processing: A slightly flattened baked (hongqing) green: fixed, rolled, first-baked, straightened, shaped and dried to set the form.
harvest_season: One bud with one or two leaves. Exact dates are little documented; as with other Shaanxi greens, spring is the main picking.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight, slightly flat strands with a swallow-tail shape, jade green with visible down.
appearance_wet: Tender green leaf, in keeping with its one-bud, one-or-two-leaf picking.
taste_profile: A lasting young-leaf aroma and a fresh, tender taste, mellow and clean with a sweet return.

brewing.notes: These are typical settings for a baked Chinese green. A glass shows off the straight, swallow-tail leaf.

vintage_note: Usually sold as the current spring's tea, as is normal for greens of its kind, and best drunk within about a year. It is a new-style regional tea rather than an ageing tea, and it is sold in only a limited number of cities.
description:
Baxian Yunwu, originally just Baxian tea, is a modern high-mountain green from the Songya area of Baxian district in Pingli county, southern Shaanxi. The name means Eight Immortals cloud and mist, after the place and its weather.

The gardens mostly sit at 1,000 to 1,400 metres in closed-in valleys, with the rain and mist the name implies. Picked at one bud with one or two leaves, the tea goes through fixing, rolling, baking, straightening and a final setting bake, and ends up tight, straight and faintly flat with a swallow-tail shape.

In the cup it is tender green and clear, with a lasting young-leaf aroma and a fresh taste that turns mellow and sweet. Slightly cooled water and a glass or porcelain cup suit it, as they do most baked greens.

It is sold in a limited market, so expect small makers. Ask for the harvest date, and check that the tea is from Pingli and not a generic yunwu, a word used across China for mountain teas.
history:
The tea was created by staff of the Pingli county tea technology station and local growers, beginning in 1984. It passed provincial appraisal in 1986 and collected Shaanxi quality titles in 1987 and 1988, then a Lu Yu Cup award at a western China tea conference in 1990.

Tea in Songya itself is said to go back further. A local story holds that a settler named Zhang brought seed from Hunan in the Kangxi period, more than 300 years ago, and planted it at the head of the Ya river. That part is tradition rather than record.
